newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq Kurd militia pursues offensive against rival.
newsitem.headline: Iraq Kurd militia pursues offensive against rival.

text.p: An Iraqi Kurdish faction that allied itself with Baghdad in late August to try to drive a rival Kurdish group out of northern Iraq said it was making progress in a new offensive.

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) said its fighters had retaken the town of Ranya and would move south to capture Sulaimaniya, the stronghold of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) near the Iranian border.

The KDP, after losing some ground earlier, appears now to have regained the initiative. PUK claims that Iraqi forces have again intervened to assist its adversary were denied by the group and could not be confirmed.
"We took the town of Ranya early this morning. We went to Ranya along three routes...flushing the PUK out as we went," said Zaim Ali, a local KDP commander, on Saturday.

"Once we clean up our Iranian border we will move our forces towards Sulaimaniya," he told Reuters in Arbil, one-time seat of a joint PUK-KDP administration that collapsed in 1994 when fighting broke out between the two groups.

The KDP took control of Arbil last month with help from Baghdad's forces and forced the PUK to abandon Sulaimaniya. But the PUK struck back this month, winning back Sulaimaniya and other towns on the route to Arbil.

An official at KDP headquarters in the town of Salahuddin said the capture of Ranya was part of a strategy to assault a series of positions near the Iranian border to cut off the PUK from what the KDP says are its Iranian allies.
KDP leader Massoud Barzani was on his way to Ranya and fighters were moving their heavy weapons towards the town.

The KDP official said its forces were attacking the PUK on two other fronts -- at Chuman close to the border with Iran and the towns of Khalakan and Kani Watman near the Dukan Dam, which supplies power to most of the area round Arbil.
A senior U.S. diplomat, Robert Pelletreau, was due to hold talks with Barzani this week -- probably in Turkey -- to try to end to the latest fighting between the two Kurdish groups.
Barzani raised the stakes by threatening to call again on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein for help against Jalal Talabani's PUK.

The Kurds broke from Baghdad at the end of the 1991 Gulf War and set up a power-sharing parliament in Arbil. The area is essentially off-limits to the Iraqi government because of a U.S.-led air operation to protect them.
Baghdad's intervention on the side of Barzani's forces last month led the United States to attack military targets in southern Iraq with cruise missiles and to extend a no-fly zone there.
